Human Rabies

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Carte Blanche: Rabies is a deadly disease that has reared its head again. A recent outbreak in KwaZulu-Natal has led to the death of 4 people. We visit the province to investigate

Unique Selling Point:
Why is rabies still a disease that we cannot control or stop. It is always fatal and no-one is spared. Why is the government not able to monitor and control the recent scourge that has led to the death of 4 people and a suspected 230 confirmed cases in KwaZulu-Natal alone.


Summary:
A heartbroken father lost his three year old son when he was bitten by a stray cat on New Year’s Day at Palm Dune Resort in Blythedale on the Natal South coast. Greg Hayes and his wife and the rest of the family is devastated. At the time of the cat bite, Hayes had no idea that the cat had rabies. It took 6 weeks before the boy fell ill and died within one week. His death on the 17th of February led to an enquiry. Hayes then traced back their movements over the last 2 months to the cat which bit their little boy and they suspected had rabies. An autopsy confirmed his suspicion.
For Npandbo Mchunu, a father from Richards Bay, the traumatic event of losing his 6 year old Ianda Nxosi was something he do not wish on any other father. The father tells the story: “The boy came back from visiting his relatives up north and he became ill thereafter. I took him to the local hospital in Empaneni and they kept him there, said he had the rabies disease.” He never came back home. He died in that hospital,” he says.




Further information:
Rabies is a deadly disease and always fatal if not treated immediately. A recent spike in KwaZulu-Natal has lead to a heightened awareness of the severity of the uncontrollable rapid spread to various parts of the province.

“Rabies kills everything, 100% and it is not something you mess with,” says State Vet, Dr. Kevin Le Roux, who leads the Rabies project for the Department of Agriculture and Rural Development in KZN. The numbers he quote is staggering: “In KZN alone, around 70 000 people are being treated for rabies in response to being bitten by an animal suspected to be rabid (have rabies)”, 4 human rabies deaths this year alone and 53 confirmed cases.

He said it is a very clever virus living in the animal as often a person will try to help an animal they think is in distress, the animal will then turn on them and in that way they contract the disease. Unless you know the history of the animal, he warns, to always seek medical help immediately.

MEC for the Department, Themba Mthembu, says they are doing what KZN has the best rabies treatment programme in Africa and that they are busy with a rabies awareness campaign visiting schools and handing out marketing material. Mthembu recons they are handling the crisis well.

DA spokesperson in KZN on Agriculture and Rural Development, Sizwe Mchunu says this is not so and are demanding answers as to what measures are in place, what are the true numbers of the rabies related cases since the start of 2018 and how does the department intend to control and monitor the disease effectively to avoid further human loss.

Rabies injections are very costly. It could cost up to R10 000 for treatment of severe cases in a private hospital. Most indigent patients however will get free treatment from a state hospital. Dr. Fiandero, a specialist in emergency care from the Mediclinic in Pietermaritzburg will explain in detail the treatment process, cost, and effectivity if caught in time.

In South Africa, unlike the rest of the world, rabies falls under the animal act whereas in the rest of the world it falls under the human control act. Dr. Keith Perrrit is chairman of the Rabies Advisory Group (RAG), a national initiative to address rabies and work together with the various governmental departments including the Department of Health, Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, and the National Institute for Communicable Diseases. It’s main function is to advisee Veterinary services on rabies matters, the control and the control thereof.

Dr. Vanessa Meyer started a campaign called the Rabies Awareness Body in eShowe with the key focus to go into local communities and inoculate pets and provide educational material. She feels too little is done on national level and through her small circle of volunteers she provides free rabies injections as a way to stop the spread in the northern part of KZN. Through social media she also spread the word and provide educational material. We spend a day with her on one of her visits to the Sunnydale community outside eShowe where she will spend a day administering rabie injections to all dog and cat owners who cannot afford it.

More information:
Rabies typically begin 20 - 60 days after exposure but could also be months which makes it difficult to relate the dog bite or a lick to the symptoms. Early symptoms of rabies are vague but could include fever, headache, sore throat, fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting. An early clue is itching or tingling at the site of the animal bite. The usual cause of death is difficulty in breathing and eventually heart failure.

Rabies is recognised by the symptoms and signs. If you don’t report a recent dog bite it can be extremely difficult to identify rabies in the early stages. Often the disease is only confirmed after death. By law post-mortem examination is required in cases of suspected rabies. Typical changes in the brain will confirm the diagnosis. If rabies is suspected before the person dies, an attempt may be made to identify the virus in a skin sample or in cells from the cornea of the eye. It is possible to grow the virus from saliva in specialised laboratories with special safety facility. A blood test can be done to detect antibodies to the rabies virus, but this will only become positive late in the diseases. In South Africa, all rabies testing for humans is done at the National Institute for Communicable Diseases in Johannesburg.

Press Release:


Human Rabies
It’s a brutal disease with fatal consequences. A rabies outbreak has once again reared its head in KwaZulu-Natal. This has led to the death of 4 people including its youngest victim, a 3-year-old boy who died after being scratched by a rabid stray cat. Carte Blanche asks: why has government failed to control the scourge?


Script:


Script: Human Rabies
Date: 4 April 2018

V/O KwaZulu-Natal is in a crisis. Rabies has spiraled out of control.
148 Animals and 4 people have died of rabies since the beginning of the year. Kevin Le Roux heads the Rabies project in the province for the department.

Kevin Le Roux: Rabies Project Manager - Veterinary services KZN Agriculture and Rural Development: Rabies is the most deadly disease known to man and if you don’t get treated immediately within the first 24 to 48 hours you could die. It kills 100%.

Claire Mawisa: Would you describe this as a crisis in Kzn?

Kevin Le Roux: Absolutely! With a 400% increase in animals with rabies, from going to no people dying at the end of last year to 4 people. There has got to be more people that we don’t know about.

V/O Rabies is a silent killer. Often not detected until it is too late. Children are most at risk as they are in close proximity to pets. Dr. Daniel Fiandeiro has been treating human rabies in the Pietermaritzburg area. He explains how rabies enters the body.

Dr. Daniel Fiandeiro: Emergency specialist - Mediclinic Pietermaritzburg: Often you get the bite, sometimes it is not that obvious, a puppy that has licked your wound so often there is no symptom at that point. Basically it gets into the wound it starts to multiply in that wound there is absolutely no symptoms. It slowly gets into your nervous system. The moment it gets into the central nervous system you start showing symptoms.

Claire Mawisa: is rabies 100% fatal.

Dr. Daniel Fiandero: It is 100% fatal, 100% preventable.

Up audio: Raben puppy in distress

Kevin Le Roux: The dog is the perfect host specie It can spread very effectively amongst them. And then every mammal can be infected and die of rabies.

Claire Mawisa: What are the symptoms in animals?

Kevin Le Roux: There is a vast array of symptoms that goes from mild agitation right through to aggression to total paralysis and death and that normally happens in about 3 days.

Up audio: Raben calf showing agitation

Kevin Le Roux: Pet owners have to vaccinate their pets by law but they don’t. Veterinary services constitute 180 people to service 10 million people it is almost an impossible task.

Vanessa Meyer: What’s his name?

Boy: Spike.

V/O Vanessa Meyer, a vet from eShowe, is aware of the crisis and offered her services to the state in her spare time. Together with a group of volunteers she has vaccinated over 200 animals since the outbreak in the province.

Up audio: Loudspeaker: Zulu announcer on loudspeaker

Vanessa Meyer: The department of Agriculture is really pressed for reaching all the people. So we just to try and take a load off them. Every bit helps.

V/O But it is the death of people that makes everyone sits up and take notice. Not far from where Meyer and her team have been working, sadly one life was lost. In a small village of Enseleni outside Richards Bay, a father tells us his story.

Ntando Mchunu: Father of rabies victim: (subtitles) His name was Ayanda Nkhosi. Another name we called him by was Wandile.

V/O Ayanda fell ill after a visit to family in December. On his return in February the signs of rabies was already evident in his behaviour.

Ntando Mchunu: (subtitles) When I arrived where he was, I saw that his body had lost weight. He would talk but the wrong words would come out, like his tongue did not want to talk. He said he could see people wanting to kill him. Serious, he said: “daddy these people they want to kill me.” Then he would cry. Towards his end, he told us he was out of energy. That’s when we took him to hospital.

Claire Mawisa: And then what happened at the hospital?

Ntando Mchunu: (subtitles) They said they thought it was rabies.

V/O Rabies attacks the nervous system and enters brain causing hallucinations and aggressive behaviour.

Dr. Daniel Fiandeiro: We are looking at patients who are terrified, patients who are hallucinating, some of the most horrific symptoms. The child just starts to almost become absolutely wild.

Claire Mawisa: (subtitles) So when he was in hospital, when he was sick, what did he look like, other than losing weight? Was he shouting, was he violent, was he fighting with people?

Ntando Mchunu: (subtitles) He fought and bit as well. If anyone tried to touch him, especially near his mouth, he’d bite. He also fought a lot because the hospital had him tied, when we arrived they tied him.

Claire Mawisa: (subtitles) When you went to go see him in hospital, when they had restrained him, how did that make you feel?

Ntando Mchunu: (subtitles) Ah it was painful.

V/O Ayanda Nkhosi died on 15 February. In a biopsy of his brain, the doctors confirmed that it was rabies. Four days later, another boy died in Kloof near Pietermaritzburg. Three year old Ethan Hays was attacked by a cat at Palm Dune Beach Lodge in Blythedale in January this year.

Greg Hayes: Father of victim: On the first of January my son and I were walking back from the swimming pool to our room to have a bit of a rest. A cat came out of the blue and clinched onto my son’s leg and scratched him quite badly on his leg.

V/O Hayes was told that the cats on the premises were part of a feral cat feeding programme. Not knowing the status of the wild cats he erred on the side of caution and reported the incident to the receptionist.

Greg Hayes: I said my son has been attacked by a cat do I need to go and get a tetanus shot done or any treatment and she assured me that all the cats on the resort has been treated I have got nothing to worry about.

V/O Then about three weeks later little Ethan fell ill with flu-like symptoms.

Dr. Daniel Fiandeiro: The first symptom obviously there is a development of numbness and pain generally around where the bite was now this can develop anything from 10 days to 19 years. And all of a sudden you get this numbness and pain quickly develop to something like flu-like symptoms, so fevers, aches, headaches, nausea, on to aggression, hyper-salivation, right into a coma.

Greg Hayes: The doctor diagnosed it as a severe sinus infection. He gave him strong antibiotics and said if he is not better within 2 days please come back.

V/O Ethan did not get better and was admitted to hospital for dehydration.

Greg Hayes: After a couple of hours in the paediatric ward he started hallucinating saying that “daddy the monsters are coming the monsters are coming and even at times he said to his mother: “where is mommy, where is mommy?”

V/O Ethan was put into an induced coma to keep him calm.

Greg Hayes: He did get aggressive so when they tried to put him under he attacked two nurses, he scratched them, he bit his mother and he bit the one nurse on the face.

V/O Several tests were done and an MRI scan, but nothing was conclusive. Then Hayes told the doctors about the cat attack in January and they suspected rabies. By then it was too late to save Ethan. He died on 19 February.

Greg Hayes: Five days later we were informed that my son did have rabies and my whole family including 20 nurses in the hospital all had to be treated for rabies.

Claire Mawisa: Is it tricky to diagnose?

Dr. Fiandeiro; It absolutely is! Literally you have a child that long forgotten about the exposure. Also the tests are very hard to do. So to try and confirm it is very hard.

V/O A state vet informed Hayes that a dead cat was found in reception at Palm Dune Beach Lodge round about the same time that his son died. We asked the owner, Brad Rayson for comment. In an email response he said that his insurance company is reviewing the matter in the event of a public liability claim. They have passed it onto legal.

Greg Hayes: His sisters are asking for him all the time. My one daughter is sleeping in his bed. We explain he is in heaven but they are constantly asking. We are going away in April on holiday and they are constantly asking if Ethan can come with us.

V/O With four confirmed cases and many more suspected the Department of Agriculture and Rural Development has come under fire. DA Spokesperson, Sizwe Mchunu says the the MEC has let the people down.

Sizwe Mchunu: DA Spokesperson - KZN Agriculture and Rural Development
Sizwe Mchunu: The fact that it has led to deaths means that there is a crisis. But secondly whilst there are people who has lost their lives and we have a department that has not been able to come out to the public and presents its account of the situation and how it intends dealing with it renders the whole situation into a state of crisis.

V/O Themba Mthembu, MEC - KZN Agriculture and Rural Development cancelled our interview and a scheduled press conference due to an emergency meeting. He has not replied to our questions sent on email.

Music up

V/O Two innocent children have lost their lives in the most horrific way. How many more people have to die before government will be able t eradicate the disease once and for all.

___________________________________________________________

PROMOS

10 seconds: A recent outbreak of rabies in KZN has led to the death of 4 people. Why is government not able to control this disease?

15 seconds:
V/O Human rabies is a silent killer, only detected when it is too late to treat.
Greg Hayes: My son lived a perfect life for one month with no sign at all and then all of a sudden got sick and died.

15 seconds;
V/O KwaZulu-Natal is in a crisis. Rabies has spiraled out of control.
Kevin le Roux: Rabies is the most deadly disease known to man and if you don’t get treated immediately within the first 24 to 48 hours you could die. It kills 100%.

That’s when we took him to hospital. Claire Mawisa: And then what happened at the hospital? Ntando Mchunu: (subtitles) They said they thought it was rabies. V/O Rabies attacks the nervous system and enters brain causing hallucinations and aggressive behaviour. Dr. Daniel Fiandeiro: We are looking at patients who are terrified, patients who are hallucinating, some of the most horrific symptoms. The child just starts to almost become absolutely wild. Claire Mawisa: (subtitles) So when he was in hospital, when he was sick, what did he look like, other than losing weight? Was he shouting, was he violent, was he fighting with people? Ntando Mchunu: (subtitles) He fought and bit as well. If anyone tried to touch him, especially near his mouth, he’d bite. He also fought a lot because the hospital had him tied, when we arrived they tied him. Claire Mawisa: (subtitles) When you went to go see him in hospital, when they had restrained him, how did that make you feel? Ntando Mchunu: (subtitles) Ah it was painful. V/O Ayanda Nkhosi died on 15 February. In a biopsy of his brain, the doctors confirmed that it was rabies. Four days later, another boy died in Kloof near Pietermaritzburg. Three year old Ethan Hays was attacked by a cat at Palm Dune Beach Lodge in Blythedale in January this year. Greg Hayes: Father of victim: On the first of January my son and I were walking back from the swimming pool to our room to have a bit of a rest. A cat came out of the blue and clinched onto my son’s leg and scratched him quite badly on his leg. V/O Hayes was told that the cats on the premises were part of a feral cat feeding programme. Not knowing the status of the wild cats he erred on the side of caution and reported the incident to the receptionist. Greg Hayes: I said my son has been attacked by a cat do I need to go and get a tetanus shot done or any treatment and she assured me that all the cats on the resort has been treated I have got nothing to worry about. V/O Then about three weeks later little Ethan fell ill with flu-like symptoms. Dr. Daniel Fiandeiro: The first symptom obviously there is a development of numbness and pain generally around where the bite was now this can develop anything from 10 days to 19 years. And all of a sudden you get this numbness and pain quickly develop to something like flu-like symptoms, so fevers, aches, headaches, nausea, on to aggression, hyper-salivation, right into a coma. Greg Hayes: The doctor diagnosed it as a severe sinus infection. He gave him strong antibiotics and said if he is not better within 2 days please come back. V/O Ethan did not get better and was admitted to hospital for dehydration. Greg Hayes: After a couple of hours in the paediatric ward he started hallucinating saying that “daddy the monsters are coming the monsters are coming and even at times he said to his mother: “where is mommy, where is mommy?” V/O Ethan was put into an induced coma to keep him calm. Greg Hayes: He did get aggressive so when they tried to put him under he attacked two nurses, he scratched them, he bit his mother and he bit the one nurse on the face. V/O Several tests were done and an MRI scan, but nothing was conclusive. Then Hayes told the doctors about the cat attack in January and they suspected rabies. By then it was too late to save Ethan. He died on 19 February. Greg Hayes: Five days later we were informed that my son did have rabies and my whole family including 20 nurses in the hospital all had to be treated for rabies. Claire Mawisa: Is it tricky to diagnose? Dr. Fiandeiro; It absolutely is! Literally you have a child that long forgotten about the exposure. Also the tests are very hard to do. So to try and confirm it is very hard. V/O A state vet informed Hayes that a dead cat was found in reception at Palm Dune Beach Lodge round about the same time that his son died. We asked the owner, Brad Rayson for comment. In an email response he said that his insurance company is reviewing the matter in the event of a public liability claim. They have passed it onto legal. Greg Hayes: His sisters are asking for him all the time. My one daughter is sleeping in his bed. We explain he is in heaven but they are constantly asking. We are going away in April on holiday and they are constantly asking if Ethan can come with us. V/O With four confirmed cases and many more suspected the Department of Agriculture and Rural Development has come under fire. DA Spokesperson, Sizwe Mchunu says the the MEC has let the people down. Sizwe Mchunu: DA Spokesperson - KZN Agriculture and Rural Development Sizwe Mchunu: The fact that it has led to deaths means that there is a crisis. But secondly whilst there are people who has lost their lives and we have a department that has not been able to come out to the public and presents its account of the situation and how it intends dealing with it renders the whole situation into a state of crisis. V/O Themba Mthembu, MEC - KZN Agriculture and Rural Development cancelled our interview and a scheduled press conference due to an emergency meeting. He has not replied to our questions sent on email. Music up V/O Two innocent children have lost their lives in the most horrific way. How many more people have to die before government will be able t eradicate the disease once and for all. ___________________________________________________________ PROMOS 10 seconds: A recent outbreak of rabies in KZN has led to the death of 4 people. Why is government not able to control this disease? 15 seconds: V/O Human rabies is a silent killer, only detected when it is too late to treat. Greg Hayes: My son lived a perfect life for one month with no sign at all and then all of a sudden got sick and died. 15 seconds; V/O KwaZulu-Natal is in a crisis. Rabies has spiraled out of control. Kevin le Roux: Rabies is the most deadly disease known to man and if you don’t get treated immediately within the first 24 to 48 hours you could die. It kills 100%.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight on Carte Blanche: Rabies is a deadly disease that has reared its head again. A recent outbreak in KwaZulu-Natal has led to the death of 4 people. We visit the province to investigate
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Why is rabies still a disease that we cannot control or stop. It is always fatal and no-one is spared. Why is the government not able to monitor and control the recent scourge that has led to the death of 4 people and a suspected 230 confirmed cases in KwaZulu-Natal alone.
metadata.Summary: A heartbroken father lost his three year old son when he was bitten by a stray cat on New Year’s Day at Palm Dune Resort in Blythedale on the Natal South coast. Greg Hayes and his wife and the rest of the family is devastated. At the time of the cat bite, Hayes had no idea that the cat had rabies. It took 6 weeks before the boy fell ill and died within one week. His death on the 17th of February led to an enquiry. Hayes then traced back their movements over the last 2 months to the cat which bit their little boy and they suspected had rabies. An autopsy confirmed his suspicion. For Npandbo Mchunu, a father from Richards Bay, the traumatic event of losing his 6 year old Ianda Nxosi was something he do not wish on any other father. The father tells the story: “The boy came back from visiting his relatives up north and he became ill thereafter. I took him to the local hospital in Empaneni and they kept him there, said he had the rabies disease.” He never came back home. He died in that hospital,” he says.
metadata.Further information: Rabies is a deadly disease and always fatal if not treated immediately. A recent spike in KwaZulu-Natal has lead to a heightened awareness of the severity of the uncontrollable rapid spread to various parts of the province. “Rabies kills everything, 100% and it is not something you mess with,” says State Vet, Dr. Kevin Le Roux, who leads the Rabies project for the Department of Agriculture and Rural Development in KZN. The numbers he quote is staggering: “In KZN alone, around 70 000 people are being treated for rabies in response to being bitten by an animal suspected to be rabid (have rabies)”, 4 human rabies deaths this year alone and 53 confirmed cases. He said it is a very clever virus living in the animal as often a person will try to help an animal they think is in distress, the animal will then turn on them and in that way they contract the disease. Unless you know the history of the animal, he warns, to always seek medical help immediately. MEC for the Department, Themba Mthembu, says they are doing what KZN has the best rabies treatment programme in Africa and that they are busy with a rabies awareness campaign visiting schools and handing out marketing material. Mthembu recons they are handling the crisis well. DA spokesperson in KZN on Agriculture and Rural Development, Sizwe Mchunu says this is not so and are demanding answers as to what measures are in place, what are the true numbers of the rabies related cases since the start of 2018 and how does the department intend to control and monitor the disease effectively to avoid further human loss. Rabies injections are very costly. It could cost up to R10 000 for treatment of severe cases in a private hospital. Most indigent patients however will get free treatment from a state hospital. Dr. Fiandero, a specialist in emergency care from the Mediclinic in Pietermaritzburg will explain in detail the treatment process, cost, and effectivity if caught in time. In South Africa, unlike the rest of the world, rabies falls under the animal act whereas in the rest of the world it falls under the human control act. Dr. Keith Perrrit is chairman of the Rabies Advisory Group (RAG), a national initiative to address rabies and work together with the various governmental departments including the Department of Health, Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, and the National Institute for Communicable Diseases. It’s main function is to advisee Veterinary services on rabies matters, the control and the control thereof. Dr. Vanessa Meyer started a campaign called the Rabies Awareness Body in eShowe with the key focus to go into local communities and inoculate pets and provide educational material. She feels too little is done on national level and through her small circle of volunteers she provides free rabies injections as a way to stop the spread in the northern part of KZN. Through social media she also spread the word and provide educational material. We spend a day with her on one of her visits to the Sunnydale community outside eShowe where she will spend a day administering rabie injections to all dog and cat owners who cannot afford it. More information: Rabies typically begin 20 - 60 days after exposure but could also be months which makes it difficult to relate the dog bite or a lick to the symptoms. Early symptoms of rabies are vague but could include fever, headache, sore throat, fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting. An early clue is itching or tingling at the site of the animal bite. The usual cause of death is difficulty in breathing and eventually heart failure. Rabies is recognised by the symptoms and signs. If you don’t report a recent dog bite it can be extremely difficult to identify rabies in the early stages. Often the disease is only confirmed after death. By law post-mortem examination is required in cases of suspected rabies. Typical changes in the brain will confirm the diagnosis. If rabies is suspected before the person dies, an attempt may be made to identify the virus in a skin sample or in cells from the cornea of the eye. It is possible to grow the virus from saliva in specialised laboratories with special safety facility. A blood test can be done to detect antibodies to the rabies virus, but this will only become positive late in the diseases. In South Africa, all rabies testing for humans is done at the National Institute for Communicable Diseases in Johannesburg.
